column2: A horizontal bar chart that plots tasks against a timeline, showing start, duration, and finish for each.
A visual board with columns for workflow stages (e.g. To Do, Doing, Done) where tasks move as cards from left to right.
Work Breakdown Structure — a hierarchical decomposition of a project's total scope into smaller, manageable work packages.
The longest sequence of dependent tasks in a project; it sets the shortest possible project duration.
The amount of time a task can be delayed without pushing back the project's finish date.
A zero-duration marker for a significant point or event in a project, such as a phase completion.

column1: What is a dependency in scheduling?
column2: A logical relationship that determines the order in which two tasks must occur.

column1: What are the four types of task dependency?
column2: Finish-to-Start, Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish, and Start-to-Finish.
A network diagram showing tasks and dependencies, often used with three time estimates (optimistic, pessimistic, most likely) to model uncertainty.

column1: What is the difference between a Gantt chart and a network diagram?
column2: A Gantt chart plots tasks against time; a network diagram plots tasks by logical sequence and dependency, without a time axis.

column1: What is a baseline in project management?
column2: The originally approved version of the schedule, budget, or scope, used as a fixed reference to measure actual performance against.
Uncontrolled expansion of a project's scope without corresponding adjustments to time, cost, or resources.
A responsibility-assignment chart marking each task as Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, or Informed for every stakeholder.
Adjusting a schedule to resolve over-allocation, so no resource is assigned more work than its available capacity.
Compressing a schedule by running tasks in parallel that were originally planned in sequence.
Compressing a schedule by adding resources to critical-path tasks, usually at extra cost.
A log of identified project risks, their likelihood, impact, and the response planned for each.
A tracking log for Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies, kept alongside the schedule.
A document listing everyone with an interest in the project, along with their influence and communication needs.
A short document that formally authorizes a project and names its objectives, scope, and project manager.
The lowest level of a WBS — a task small enough to be assigned, scheduled, and tracked directly.
A method for measuring project performance by comparing planned work, actual work done, and actual cost.

column1: What do PV, EV, and AC stand for in EVM?
column2: Planned Value, Earned Value, and Actual Cost.
Cost Performance Index — earned value divided by actual cost; below 1 means the project is over budget.
Schedule Performance Index — earned value divided by planned value; below 1 means the project is behind schedule.
A chart showing remaining work versus time in a sprint or project, used in Agile to track progress toward completion.
A chart showing completed work and total scope over time, useful for visualizing scope changes alongside progress.

column1: What is a sprint in Scrum?
column2: A fixed, short time-box, typically one to four weeks, in which a defined set of work is completed.
An ordered list of everything that might be needed in the product, maintained and prioritized by the product owner.
The subset of backlog items selected for the current sprint, along with the plan for delivering them.
The amount of work a team completes per sprint, usually measured in story points, used to forecast future capacity.
A short daily meeting where each team member states what was done, what is planned next, and any blockers.

column1: What is the difference between Waterfall and Agile?
column2: Waterfall plans and executes phases sequentially with fixed scope; Agile delivers work in short iterative cycles with scope that can adapt.
A structured project management method built around defined stages, defined roles, and a business-case-driven approach, widely used in the UK and government projects.
A Project Management Institute publication describing standard project management processes, knowledge areas, and terminology.

column1: What is a Definition of Done?
column2: An agreed checklist of conditions a piece of work must meet before it can be counted as complete.

column1: What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?
column2: The smallest version of a product that can be released to validate an idea with real users.

column1: What is a change control process?
column2: A formal procedure for proposing, reviewing, approving, and recording changes to a project's scope, schedule, or budget.

column1: What is a status report used for?
column2: Communicating progress, risks, and upcoming work to stakeholders at a regular cadence.
The first project meeting, used to align the team and stakeholders on objectives, scope, roles, and schedule.
The process of assigning available people, equipment, and budget to specific project tasks.

column1: What is the difference between a program and a project?
column2: A project is a temporary effort with a defined outcome; a program is a group of related projects managed together for shared benefits.

column1: What is a portfolio in project management?
column2: A collection of projects and programs grouped together to meet strategic business objectives, not necessarily related to each other directly.

column1: What is a Gantt chart's main limitation for large projects?
column2: It can become cluttered and hard to read once the number of tasks and dependencies grows large.

column1: Why do many teams use Kanban instead of Gantt charts for ongoing work?
column2: Kanban suits continuous, unscheduled flow of work better than a fixed timeline, which fits projects with a defined start and end.

column1: What is a swimlane on a Kanban board?
column2: A horizontal row used to separate tasks by category, team, or priority, layered on top of the usual workflow columns.

column1: What is a WIP limit in Kanban?
column2: A cap on the number of tasks allowed in a given workflow stage at once, used to prevent overload and expose bottlenecks.

column1: What is the difference between a task and a deliverable?
column2: A task is an activity performed; a deliverable is the tangible or intangible output produced by one or more tasks.
A meeting held after a project or sprint to review what went well, what did not, and what should change next time.

column1: What is the difference between a project manager and a product owner?
column2: A project manager is responsible for delivering the project's schedule, budget, and scope; a product owner is responsible for prioritizing what gets built, most common in Agile/Scrum settings.
